title: refusing the tag operation leaves the panic name resolvable: panic and its const alias still call and still return, and three ordinary tags — one of them named panic — still run
notes: specification/failures.mdx (Locked): '`panic` is imported from `smithers:exceptions` and accepts an optional message or underlying Error' and 'Calling `panic(...)` MUST NOT force a function's return type to widen into `Result<A, Panic>`'. The rule its sibling `the-panic-intrinsic-is-a-call-and-not-a-template-tag` applies refuses the tag OPERATION; it must leave the NAME resolvable, which is `SMITHERS1604`'s settled shape. So `panic` stays importable, stays callable in a supported placement, stays assignable to a `const`, and an unrelated tag that merely happens to be named `panic` stays an ordinary tagged template. WHY THIS CASE IS NOT DECORATION: without it, its sibling can be made green by widening the rule to 'any tag whose name is `panic`', and this repository has shipped TEN over-corrections. The single revision behind this pair removed 13 reference over-refusals on programs that run, so the over-correction direction is the measured one, not the hypothetical one. Five spellings, and the two that carry the guard are `panicTag` — a LOCAL function whose name contains the intrinsic's letters — and `local.panic`, a local object member literally NAMED `panic` in the same member-tag position as the ambient `Reflect.panic` the sibling refuses at 30:5. A rule that looked at the member name rather than at the ambient `Reflect` object would refuse this program; a rule that looked at the identifier text would refuse both. `String.raw` is the third-party control. WHAT THE FIRST TWO LINES PIN: `force` and `forceAliased` call `panic(...)` in the supported expression-statement placement on a branch that is not taken, and both return normally, so the output shows that refusing the tag did not disturb the call, the alias binding, or the plain return type the specification's non-widening rule requires. The distinct join separators — `|` for `panicTag`, `/` for `local.panic` — are why each tag's single-part output is its own letter rather than a shared one, so a resolver that reordered or dropped a tag produces a visible permutation instead of an invisible one. WHAT IT DOES NOT PIN: the panic MESSAGE, which is observed instead by `explicit-panic-charges-the-channel` and `reflect-panic-enters-the-panic-channel` (both declare `panic: no entry for zoe` in `stdout`); those two are the controls that keep `panic("x")` carrying its authored message across this revision, and both stayed green. Nor does it pin the `/** @throws {never} */` on `panicTag`, which is INERT here and was measured so rather than assumed: a throwaway copy of this program without it produces the same five lines on both backends. It is kept because it is the annotation `failures.mdx` names at a boundary that cannot fail, and dropping it would invite the reader to conclude something this case did not measure. VERIFIED LOAD-BEARING, not assumed: mutating the FOURTH declared stdout line from `b` to `c` turns the case red on BOTH backends with `["ada","ada","a","b","c"] != ["ada","ada","a","c","c"]` printed on each. The fourth line is chosen because it is `local.panic`b``, the object member literally NAMED `panic`: it is the one line whose absence from the observation would leave a name-keyed over-correction unguarded, which is the specific way this case's sibling could be made green for the wrong reason. The mutator refuses to run at all unless the case is green on BOTH backends first AND its search string occurs exactly once in the file; both refusals were exercised against this case rather than assumed, because a search string that matches nothing mutates nothing and comes back green.
